intro: Pasted text changes fonts in Word for Mac because the copied text carries its formatting with it. The copy holds the source font, size, colour and links, and Word can keep all of them. The fix is usually a different paste, not a different font, and you can make that change in about ten seconds.
tldr: Copied text carries a rich version of its formatting, and Word may keep it.
Web pages can name fonts your Mac does not have, so Word swaps in a substitute.
Paste with Keep Text Only in Word, or use the Paste Options button after a paste.
Clear pasted formatting on the text itself, because a theme change often leaves it in place.

blocks.text: Why pasted text brings its font with it

When you copy text on a Mac, the copy does not hold just the words. It holds the text in several versions at once. A web browser usually adds an HTML version. A desktop app often adds RTF, which stands for rich text format. Each version can carry the font family, size, colour, bold, italic and links.

When you paste, the receiving app chooses one version. If it chooses a rich version, the formatting lands with the words. Each app has its own rules for which version to take. The same copy can behave differently in Word, Pages and Google Docs. That is why a paste that looks clean in Notes can look wrong in Word.
What Keep Source Formatting does in Word

In Word, the setting behind most font surprises is Keep Source Formatting. Microsoft's support page says this option keeps the copied formatting. It also copies any associated style definition into your document. Your file then holds the source's style, not just its words.

The default is disputed, so check your own copy. Office Watch, dated 13 January 2026, says Keep Source Formatting is the default for pasting from other programs. A Windows Central headline says Microsoft changed the default to Merge Formatting. The full Windows Central article was not available to confirm that claim.

blocks.title: Check your paste setting
blocks.text: Microsoft documents the paste settings under File > Options > Advanced > Cut, copy, and paste. That path is for Windows. On a Mac, search Word's Help for cut, copy, and paste to find the matching setting for your version.
The four paste options, side by side

rows: Source font, size, colour and the style definition
Copying a styled block you want to match exactly
Bold and italic, plus the destination's style
Web text that should match your document
A picture of the content, Microsoft 365 only
Content you do not need to edit
Quotes, notes and text that must match your style
blocks.caption: Paste options in Word, as listed on Microsoft's support page.

blocks.text: Microsoft says the Paste Options button appears after a paste by default. Click it and choose a different setting for the same paste. You do not need to copy the text again. That saves time when the first paste looks wrong.
Worked example: three pastes, three choices

Say you are writing a grant report on your Mac. You copy three things. The first is a paragraph from a government web page. The second is a table from another Word file. The third is a quote you read in a PDF.

For the web paragraph, choose Merge Formatting or Keep Text Only. Merge keeps bold and italic, then takes the destination's style. Keep Text Only gives plain words in your style. If the page font does not matter, pick Keep Text Only.

For the table, choose Keep Source Formatting if the table must keep its look. Choose Merge Formatting if the table must match your report. After either choice, check every number against the source file.
For the PDF quote, choose Keep Text Only, then add the quote marks yourself. Plain text carries no font at all, so the quote matches your body text.
Web fonts: why a font name can arrive without the font

A web page can name a font that loads from the web. Your Mac may not have that font installed. When you paste, the name can come along in the clipboard, but the font file does not. Word then uses an installed font, so the text looks close but not quite right.

Say a blog post sets its body text in a font called Acme Serif. You never installed Acme Serif. The pasted paragraph shows a different serif, and the name Acme Serif still sits in its formatting. Nothing on the page warns you.

blocks.title: Shared files
blocks.text: A file with substituted fonts can look different on another Mac. Your reviewer sees whatever font their Mac picks. Check the file on a second machine, or send a PDF when the layout matters.
Why changing the theme does not fix pasted fonts

A common first move is to change the theme or the Normal style. That works for text you typed. It often fails for pasted text. Edge Drop reports that pasted font names persist after a theme or style change.

The reason is direct formatting. The font sits on the characters themselves, not in the style. A style change does not override direct formatting. You have to clear the formatting on the text, or replace the text.
Edge Drop says Ctrl+Space clears character formatting in Word on Windows. Word for Mac may use a different shortcut. Check Word's keyboard shortcut list on your Mac before you rely on it.
Fix 1: paste as plain text in Word for Mac
Use Keep Text Only for the cleanest result. Office Watch says Keep Text Only has the shortcut Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+V in Word 365 for Windows and Mac. On a Mac, that is ⇧⌘V.

items: Copy the text as usual with ⌘C.
Click where the text belongs in your document.
Press ⇧⌘V to paste as Keep Text Only.
Check the font in the Font box on the Home tab.

blocks.text: If the shortcut does nothing, your version of Word may differ. Use the Paste Options button instead. The next section shows how.
Fix 2: use Paste Options and Merge Formatting

Paste normally with ⌘V. Then click the Paste Options button near the pasted text. Choose Merge Formatting to keep bold and italic while the text takes Word's style. Choose Keep Text Only for a clean paste.
Merge Formatting is not the same as plain text. Merge removes most direct formatting, but bold and italic survive. If a link or a colour matters, check it after you choose.
Google Docs on Mac: paste without formatting

Google Docs uses ⇧⌘V for Paste without formatting on Mac. Google's keyboard shortcut list gives Ctrl+Shift+V for Windows and Chrome OS, and Cmd+Shift+V for Mac. Use the same shortcut on every paste until it feels automatic.

Google's list also gives ⌘⌥V for Paste text formatting. Use it when you want the look of one passage on another. Third-party sources disagree about where this option sits in the Edit menu, so use the shortcut and skip the menu hunt. For more Docs habits, see [Google Docs for writers on Mac](/for/writers/google-docs).
Pages on Mac: paste and match style
Pages has a direct fix. Apple's keyboard shortcut list gives ⌥⇧⌘V for Paste and match the style of the destination text. Use it when the text should look like the paragraph you paste into.

⌥⌘V is a different command. It pastes paragraph and cell styles, which helps with tables and lists. It also brings style names with it. Use it on purpose, not as a habit. For more Pages habits, see [Pages for writers on Mac](/for/writers/pages).
Clean up text that already landed

You already pasted it, so do not paste again on top. Select the wrong block first. Then set the font in the destination app so the text takes the look you want. Check that the headings still use heading styles.

A cleaner method is to rebuild the block. Paste the text into a plain text app such as TextEdit or Notes. Copy it again from there. Then paste into your document with Keep Text Only or Paste and match style.
Work section by section in long documents. Check one section, then move on. If you wait until the end, you cannot tell which paste caused which problem.
What this costs you, honestly

No survey measures how often writers get wrong fonts from pasted text. Nobody has counted the minutes lost. Treat the costs below as reasoned estimates, not a measured bill. The numbers here come from scientific manuscripts, which is the closest research I found.

A PLOS ONE survey of 372 respondents from 41 countries found a median of 14 hours of formatting per manuscript. That study covers manuscript formatting in general, not pasted text. Nature Index reports the same figure as an average, so check the wording before you quote it.

A related PMC study of 206 US-based biomedical researchers found that nearly 91% spend more than four hours on reformatting adjustments per manuscript. Those are scientific papers, so your Word file will likely cost less. The lesson still holds. Small fixes add up across a long document.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not
Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

Lazur points, explains and guides. Ask where the Paste Options button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to choose Keep Text Only, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate Word, Google Docs or Pages for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any of them. You still make the paste choice yourself. That is the honest split.
Writing new text so nothing arrives from a web page

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. New words typed by voice do not carry a web page's font with them. Dictation is included, and it is unlimited on both Pro and Power plans. See [pricing](/pricing) for plan details.

Snippets and clipboard slots help with text you reuse, such as a standard disclaimer or a citation format. Save the plain version once. Then paste it from the same place every time. The personal dictionary holds names and terms you want spelled the same way each time.

blocks.title: Client and patient data
blocks.text: If you are a lawyer, nurse or accountant, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you paste or dictate anything into an AI tool. Your employer's rules come first, not this page.
A worked case: fixing a long draft after a research sweep

Say you gathered quotes from a research PDF, a web article and an old Word draft. The headings look right. The body text has three fonts. You want one font and no hidden styles before an editor sees the file.

Start with the PDF quotes, since plain text fixes them fastest. Paste them with ⇧⌘V in Word, then set the body font. Next, the web article. Use Merge Formatting, then check every link. Last, the old draft. Keep its headings and clear the body text.

Check the headings after each paste so you catch changes early. If the table of contents misbehaves later, see [why Word for Mac will not update its table of contents](/for/writers/problems/word-mac-table-contents-not-updating).
Mistakes people make when they fix pasted text

items: Changing the theme and expecting pasted text to follow it.
Pasting again with ⌘V after each failed try, which adds another copy of the formatting.
Fixing only the first paragraph and trusting the rest of the document.
Choosing Keep Source Formatting because it keeps the look, then fighting the font for an hour.
Trusting a shortcut from another platform without checking Word for Mac.
Sending a file with web fonts to a reviewer without checking how it looks on their machine.

blocks.text: A habit that stops the problem for good

Pick one paste habit for each app and use it every time. In Word, use ⇧⌘V for quotes and notes. In Google Docs, use ⇧⌘V for Paste without formatting. In Pages, use ⌥⇧⌘V when you want the destination's look.

Before you send a file, run a quick check. Scroll the headings, sample three paragraphs and export a PDF. Open the PDF on another Mac if the file matters. This takes a few minutes and catches font surprises early.
Checklist before you send the file

items: Headings still use your heading styles.
Body text uses one font across all sections.
Links still work and point where you expect.
Quotes match your quote style, not the web page's.
A PDF export looks right on a second Mac.

faq.question: Why does pasted text change fonts in Word for Mac when I copy from another Word file?
faq.answer: Word can keep the source formatting when you paste from another Word document. Keep Source Formatting copies the font and the style definition into your file. Choose Keep Text Only or Merge Formatting from the Paste Options button to change that.

faq.question: Does Cmd+V keep the formatting?
faq.answer: Microsoft's page says Word keeps original formatting by default on Ctrl+V, the Paste button and right-click Paste. On a Mac, the same paste is Cmd+V. Use ⇧⌘V when you want plain words instead.

faq.question: Why does the font still change after I pick Merge Formatting?
faq.answer: Merge Formatting removes most direct formatting but keeps bold and italic, then takes the destination's style. If the font still differs, the source probably names a web font you do not have. Use Keep Text Only for that block.

faq.question: Will changing my theme fix pasted fonts?
faq.answer: Usually not. Edge Drop reports that pasted font names persist after a theme or style change. Clear the formatting on the pasted text, or paste it again as Keep Text Only.

faq.question: Does Google Docs have the same problem on Mac?
faq.answer: Pasted formatting can carry into Google Docs too. Use ⇧⌘V for Paste without formatting, or ⌘⌥V for Paste text formatting. Google's keyboard shortcut list documents both shortcuts on Mac.

faq.question: Which paste setting is Word's default on a Mac?
faq.answer: The sources disagree. Office Watch says Keep Source Formatting is the default for pasting from other programs. A Windows Central headline says Microsoft changed it to Merge Formatting. Check your own setting, then test with one paragraph.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix the fonts in my document?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you. It can circle the Paste Options button, explain a setting, or guide you one click at a time. You make the change.

costs.title: Time spent on repeat fixes
costs.text: Each fix takes seconds. Repeat it across a long document and the minutes add up. No survey measures this for pasted text. The closest data is manuscript reformatting, where a median of 14 hours per manuscript was reported.

costs.title: A file that looks wrong to other people
costs.text: A substituted font can make a proposal or client report look careless. The reader sees the font their Mac picks, not the one you chose. That costs trust in the document, even when your words are strong.

costs.title: Headings and body text that do not match
costs.text: Pasted blocks often bring their own font into a document that uses one font everywhere else. Readers notice the mismatch before they read the argument. Fixing it late means checking every section again.

costs.title: Delays when fixes come at the end
costs.text: A PMC study of scientific manuscripts says reformatting delays most publications by at least two weeks. About 20% of manuscripts waited over three months. Those are papers, not Word files, but early checks still cost less than a last-minute cleanup.

costs.title: Styles that cling to the document
costs.text: Leftover pasted styles make theme changes unreliable. You can spend an afternoon adjusting a theme that never reaches the pasted block. The cost is mostly your patience, and it is easy to underestimate.

causes.title: The clipboard holds several versions
causes.text: When you copy, the clipboard keeps the text in more than one form. Browsers usually add an HTML version. Desktop apps often add RTF. The rich versions carry font family, size, colour and links, so a paste can bring them along.

causes.title: Word may keep the source formatting
causes.text: Microsoft's support page says Keep Source Formatting keeps the copied formatting and copies the associated style definition into the document. Office Watch says it is the default for pasting from other programs. Sources disagree on the current default, so check your own setting.

causes.title: Web fonts travel as names, not files
causes.text: A web page can name a web font that your Mac does not have. The name can arrive in the paste, but the font file cannot. Word then substitutes an installed font, so the text looks almost right. Edge Drop describes this behavior in Word.

causes.title: Direct formatting survives style changes
causes.text: Pasted fonts sit on the text as direct formatting. Edge Drop reports that pasted font names persist after a theme or style change. Changing the Normal style leaves them alone, so the problem looks like a broken theme when it is leftover formatting.

causes.title: Each app lists different paste options
causes.text: Google separates Paste without formatting from Paste text formatting. Apple separates Paste and match style from the paragraph and cell style paste. Word offers four paste options on its Paste Options button. Learn the options your app offers, not just one shortcut.

fixes.title: Paste as Keep Text Only in Word
fixes.text: Use ⇧⌘V to paste as Keep Text Only. Office Watch says Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+V is the Keep Text Only shortcut in Word 365 for Windows and Mac. The text arrives as plain words, and your document style takes over. Use this for quotes, notes and any block that must match your text.

fixes.title: Use the Paste Options button
fixes.text: After a normal ⌘V, click the Paste Options button near the pasted text. Choose Merge Formatting to keep bold and italic and take Word's style. Choose Keep Text Only for a clean result. You do not need to copy the text again to try another option.

fixes.title: Use Google Docs paste without formatting
fixes.text: In Google Docs on Mac, press ⇧⌘V for Paste without formatting. Google's keyboard shortcut list documents Cmd+Shift+V for Mac. Use ⌘⌥V for Paste text formatting when you want the look of one passage on another. Use the shortcuts, not the menus.

fixes.title: Use Pages paste and match style
fixes.text: In Pages on Mac, press ⌥⇧⌘V for Paste and match the style of the destination text. Apple's keyboard shortcut list documents this command. It makes the pasted text take the look of the paragraph you paste into, which is what most writers want.

fixes.title: Clear the formatting on pasted text
fixes.text: Select the wrong block, then set the font in the destination app so the text takes the look you want. Check that headings still use heading styles. A style change alone often leaves pasted fonts in place, so clear the text itself.

fixes.title: Rebuild the block through a plain text app
fixes.text: Paste the text into TextEdit or Notes. Copy it again from there. Then paste into your document with Keep Text Only or Paste and match style. The plain text app removes the rich versions, so only clean words move on.

fixes.title: Change Word's default paste setting on purpose
fixes.text: If you paste from the web every day, change the default paste setting once. Search Word's Help for cut, copy and paste to find the setting for your version. Then test it with one web paragraph before you trust it.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Check your paste setting
plan.text: Open Word's Help and search for cut, copy and paste. Note the default for pasting from other programs. Then paste one web paragraph with ⌘V and see what arrives.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Practice Keep Text Only
plan.text: Copy three sources, one web page, one PDF and one Word file. Paste each one with ⇧⌘V. Notice which fonts disappear and which stay, then write down the difference.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set your app habits
plan.text: In Google Docs, practice ⇧⌘V until it feels automatic. In Pages, try ⌥⇧⌘V on a styled paragraph. Keep the two shortcuts on a note near your Mac.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Fix one live document
plan.text: Open a draft with mixed fonts. Select one pasted block, clear its formatting and check the headings. Note which paste caused each problem so you stop repeating it.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Test on another Mac
plan.text: Export a PDF and open it on a second Mac, or send it to a colleague with a different font set. Confirm the body font and headings match. Fix anything that still differs.
